news_drafts.headline: Flintshire achieves £0.79m underspend as social care pressures mount
news_drafts.lead: Flintshire County Council's auditors gave an unqualified opinion on the 2025/26 accounts with no concerns about the council's ability to continue operating. The council underspent by £0.790m overall, despite significant demand-led overspends: residential care for older people cost £1.763m more than budgeted, homecare £1.632m over, and out-of-county placements for people with learning disabilities £2.573m over. The council offset these through underspends in fleet services and regulatory services, and pay award savings. It achieved 96% of its planned cost reductions. Council Fund reserves rose to £17.257m, above the policy minimum of £8.985m, boosted by an additional £1.205m from Welsh Government funding that the council chose to add to reserves to build resilience against "a challenging future funding outlook". Welsh Government's funding increase of 3.8% fell below the Welsh average of 4.5%, and provided no guidance on allocations for 2027/28 onwards.

news_drafts.headline: Flintshire borrows £25m for capital spending as rates outlook shifts
news_drafts.lead: Flintshire County Council took out £25m in borrowing (Public Works Loan Board loans, the government's lending arm for councils) during 2025/26 to fund long-term capital needs, according to its Treasury Management Annual Report reviewed by the cabinet on 15 September. Treasury advisors explored early repayment options for existing PWLB loans but rejected them as the premiums were too expensive to make refinancing worthwhile. The council maintained an average interest rate of 4.09 per cent on its investment portfolio despite Bank Rate falling during the year, reflecting disciplined cash management. The Governance and Audit Committee and Cabinet identified no significant issues with the council's treasury governance or compliance, though the outlook for interest rates has shifted from downward to uncertain due to geopolitical risk in the Middle East.

findings.headline: Waste recycling infraction fine of £1.022m for 2024/25 pending Welsh Government decision, though prior years' fines of £1.204m were waived
findings.detail: Welsh Government can levy infraction fines if councils fail to meet statutory recycling targets. Charges totalling £1.204m for 2021/22-2023/24 were waived following positive recycling performance improvements. However, the council did not meet the increased 70% target in 2024/25. A further infraction fine of £1.022m could be levied; the council has presented plans to WG and the Minister is currently reviewing whether the charge will be imposed.
findings.matters: This represents an unquantified external penalty dependent on a third party (WG) decision, but at £1m would materially worsen an already tight reserve position if imposed.
findings.figures: £1.022m potential infraction fine for 2024/25; £1.204m charges for 2021/22-2023/24 waived; decision pending WG review
findings.quote: the authority did not meet the increased statutory recycling target of 70% in 2024/25, which means that a further infraction fine of £1.022m could be levied

findings.headline: NJC pay award 3.3% agreed vs 3% budgeted, requiring £0.343m funding from reserves in-year with structural impact into 2027/28
findings.detail: The council budgeted for a 3% pay award for NJC (Green Book) staff but the national employers' offer of 3.3% has now been agreed. The council must fund the £0.343m shortfall from reserves in-year if no compensatory grant is received. The paper notes budget assumptions for 2027/28 remain at 3%, meaning the new baseline will not be absorbed and future years will inherit this structural cost increase.
findings.matters: This is a structural cost increase locked into the council's ongoing expenditure base. It signals that budget planning assumptions for future years may already be out of date and future pay awards could again exceed assumptions.
findings.figures: £0.343m additional cost; 3.3% pay award agreed vs 3% budgeted; 0.3% shortfall on workforce baseline; impact continues into 2027/28 budget
findings.quote: The amount of the final award in excess of the 3% will need to be funded from reserves in the current financial year, if there is no compensatory grant allocation. The impact of the NJC pay award is an additional £0.343m, to be met by reserves and/or grant.

findings.headline: Medium term financial strategy shows additional budget requirement of £27.866m for 2027/28
findings.detail: Separate from the current year's challenges, the cabinet considered the latest MTFS projection in September identifying an additional budget requirement of £27.866m for 2027/28. This represents a substantial structural funding gap that will require solutions through spending reductions, income growth, or further reserve use. The paper states options are currently being considered with updates to follow.
findings.matters: Combined with current year reserve depletion and unconfirmed savings in 2026/27, the scale of next year's budget gap suggests the council faces a sustained period of financial stress with limited financial flexibility. The planning assumption of only 3% pay award growth for 2027/28 may also be at risk of similar underfunding as 2026/27.
findings.figures: £27.866m additional budget requirement for 2027/28; options solutions under consideration
findings.quote: Cabinet considered the latest projection for the MTFS in September which showed an additional budget requirement of £27.866m for the financial year 2027/28.

findings.headline: Holiday pay tribunal claims: 300+ live cases with current reserve of £0.254m carrying explicit risk of 'considerably more' cost
findings.detail: Following the Supreme Court judgment in Harpur Trust v Brazel (upheld July 2022), the council faces 300+ employment tribunal claims relating to holiday pay calculations for irregular-hours and term-time workers. A reserve of £0.254m is held, but the paper explicitly states the final cost carries risk of being 'considerably more'. Case management orders require compliance through January 2027.
findings.matters: This is a significant contingent liability with minimal visibility over final cost. With reserves already depleted, any unfavorable settlement or higher claim values could force further reserve drawdown or in-year spending cuts.
findings.figures: 300+ live employment tribunal claims; £0.254m held in reserve; unquantified exposure above this level
findings.quote: There is a risk that the final cost may be considerably more than the £0.254m currently held in reserves for this purpose.

findings.headline: School delegated budgets holding £4.798m in reserves deficit as at 31 March 2026, an adverse movement of £4.199m year-on-year
findings.detail: School budgets are in severe deficit, with schools collectively holding reserves in deficit of £4.798m. This has deteriorated dramatically by £4.199m compared to the prior year (31 March 2025). The council holds a centralised budget for school exit costs but notes there is 'significant risk that the approved budget is exceeded' as schools progress through redundancy processes.
findings.matters: School deficits may eventually fall to the council to address. The scale and speed of deterioration signal underlying structural issues in school funding that could create material liabilities for the council balance sheet in future years.
findings.figures: £4.798m school reserves deficit as at 31 March 2026; £4.199m adverse movement from prior year; schools currently projecting net deficit to exceed £8m by 31 March 2027
findings.quote: school earmarked reserves held on 31st March 2026 equating to an overall deficit position of (£4.798m), an adverse movement of (£4.199m) from 31st March 2025

daily_post.headline: Income misclassification found: £426,000 coded as capital grant instead of revenue.
daily_post.lead: Income misclassification distorts the revenue versus capital split and can mask the council's true spending and financing position. While isolated, it indicates a control weakness in income coding procedures that should be monitored.
